questions.q: Why can't non-human identities like service accounts use the authentication methods built for a person?
options: Non-human identities are technically incapable of connecting to any network
Cloud providers do not allow applications to authenticate under any circumstances
There's no human present in the moment of authentication to type a password, tap Face ID, or approve a push
Service accounts are always exempt from any authentication requirement
questions.explain: A script or application authenticating on its own has no person available to complete a human-oriented authentication step in real time.

questions.q: What distinguishes a managed identity from a traditional API key?
options: An API key is always more secure than a managed identity
A managed identity is issued and rotated automatically by the cloud platform, so there's no secret value to store or copy at all
A managed identity is simply an API key with a longer expiration date
A managed identity requires a human to approve every single request
questions.explain: Managed identities remove the static secret entirely — the platform vouches for the application directly instead of a developer storing a key.

options: A legacy term for a shared service account password
A permanent password assigned to a specific server for its entire lifetime
A short-lived token issued to a workload based on a trust relationship with another system, rather than a long-term credential
A biometric credential used only by human administrators
questions.explain: Workload identities generalize the managed-identity idea: short-lived, federated tokens replace long-term static credentials.

questions.q: What is the real risk of a long-lived service account credential or API key?
options: It can end up leaked in a config file, repository, or old script, and typically stays valid and exploitable until someone manually finds and revokes it
It cannot be used by any automated system, only by humans
It poses no risk as long as it is stored in plain text
It automatically expires within minutes regardless of configuration
questions.explain: A static, long-lived secret is a standing liability — its blast radius is as large as however long it sits unnoticed after leaking.

questions.q: Why are short-lived, automatically rotated credentials considered the modern answer for non-human identities?
options: If a short-lived token leaks, its exposure window closes on its own, often before the leak is even noticed
They eliminate the need for any identity verification whatsoever
They never need to be issued by a trusted platform or service
They are easier for a human to memorize than a password
questions.explain: Short-lived tokens minimize how long a leaked credential remains useful, unlike a static key that works indefinitely until revoked.
